young.html: In Socrates' time, famous teachers called sophists traveled from city to city. For a fee, they taught young men how to speak well and win arguments, so they could succeed in public life. The most famous were Protagoras and Gorgias, and Plato named a dialogue after each of them.

Socrates liked talking with them, but he kept asking a question they found uncomfortable: Is winning an argument the same as being right? A speaker can make a crowd cheer for a bad idea. Is that a good skill to have?

In the Gorgias, Socrates uses a picture. A cook and a doctor both care about food. The cook makes food taste nice; the doctor knows what food is good for you. If children had to choose between them, the cook would win every time! Socrates says a speaker who only tries to please a crowd is like the cook, not the doctor.

young.name: gb-flattery
young.cap: Socrates' map: four true arts that do good, and four imitations that only please. Tap a box.

young.html: Cook or doctor? Find three advertisements (in a magazine, on a cereal box, online with a parent). For each one, ask: is it trying to please me, or to tell me what is good for me? Is it ever both? Talk about it together.

Socrates also says something surprising: it is worse to do wrong than to have wrong done to you. Most people think the opposite. Socrates argues that doing wrong harms your own soul, the most important part of you.

full.html: This rung gathers several of Plato's early dialogues, all about virtue and the people who claimed to teach it. All are in volume 6 of the Great Books set: Charmides (on self-control), Laches (on courage), Lysis (on friendship), Euthydemus (two brothers who play word tricks), Ion (on a reciter of Homer), and the two longer dialogues named for the great sophists, the Protagoras and the Gorgias. Most were written in the 390s and 380s BC.

Protagoras of Abdera, the most famous sophist, says he teaches young men to manage their own affairs and the city's: to be good citizens. Socrates doubts that this can be taught. Protagoras replies with a story: when the gods made living things, Epimetheus gave out all the gifts (speed, claws, fur) and had nothing left for humans, so Prometheus stole fire and the arts for them. Then Zeus sent Hermes to give justice and reverence to everyone, because a city could not survive if only a few had them. That, says Protagoras, is why everyone has a say on questions of justice, and why everyone teaches it a little.
Socrates leads Protagoras toward a different picture. Most people think a person can know what is best and still do worse, overcome by pleasure or fear. Socrates asks:

full.text: …do you think that knowledge is a noble and commanding thing, which cannot be overcome, and will not allow a man, if he only knows the difference of good and evil, to do anything which is contrary to knowledge, but that wisdom will have strength to help him?
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. I, Clarendon Press

full.html: “No one does wrong willingly.” Socrates concludes that people do wrong because they misjudge what is good, the way something near looks larger than something far. If that is right, virtue is a kind of knowledge, and could be taught. By the end, Protagoras and Socrates have swapped sides on whether virtue is teachable, and Socrates says they should start again.

Gorgias of Leontini, in Sicily, was the most celebrated speaker of the age. Socrates asks what his art, rhetoric, is about. Gorgias says: persuasion, in law courts and assemblies, about right and wrong. Socrates gets him to agree that a speaker can persuade a crowd without knowing the subject, and can make a crowd believe a doctor less than himself even on medicine.
The young Polus then takes over, and Socrates sets out his map of arts and their imitations:

full.text: Cookery simulates the disguise of medicine, and pretends to know what food is the best for the body; and if the physician and the cook had to enter into a competition in which children were the judges, or men who had no more sense than children, as to which of them best understands the goodness or badness of food, the physician would be starved to death.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

full.name: gb-flattery

full.html: Polus admires powerful men who do as they like. Socrates replies with three claims that sound backward to Polus: doing wrong is worse than suffering it; a wrongdoer is better off punished than unpunished; and powerful people who do wrong have no real power, because they do not get what they truly want, which is their own good.

full.text: For I certainly think that I and you and every man do really believe, that to do is a greater evil than to suffer injustice: and not to be punished than to be punished.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

full.html: Finally Callicles, a confident Athenian politician, attacks: by nature, he says, the strong should have more, and the laws are only an invention of the weak. The good life is satisfying every desire. Socrates compares such a life to filling a leaky jar that can never be filled, and argues for an ordered, self-controlled soul. The dialogue ends with a story of judgment after death, which Socrates says he believes is true.

Thinking Socrates was against all speaking well. In the Gorgias he imagines a true rhetoric, one that tries to make listeners better, and in the Phaedrus he sketches what it would need. His target is persuasion with no concern for truth.

Can clever word tricks teach wisdom?
Two brothers win every argument with silly puns; Socrates shows real reasoning instead.
Do poets know what they talk about?
Socrates says poets and reciters are inspired, like iron rings hanging from a magnet, more than skilled.

deep.html: The sophists were real teachers, and modern historians are kinder to them than Plato was: they taught grammar, speaking and argument to many, and some raised serious questions about whether laws are natural or made by people. Protagoras' myth is an early argument for why every citizen, not only experts, may speak on matters of justice. Plato's Socrates insists instead that speaking must answer to truth and to what is good.

Aristotle, later on this ladder, answered both. His Rhetoric treats persuasion as a real art that a good person should know, and his Ethics discusses weakness of will (akrasia), disagreeing with Socrates that it is impossible to know the better and do the worse. Callicles' idea that the strong deserve more is close to the view Thrasymachus defends in the first book of the Republic.

items: Is it really worse to do wrong than to suffer it? What would convince you either way?
Can a person know what is right and still do wrong? Have you ever done that?
Should persuasive speaking be taught to everyone? What could go wrong, and what could go right?

questions: Socrates says a cook who only pleases is different from a doctor who helps. Can you think of things that please you but aren't good for you, and things that are good for you but don't please you at first?
Is winning an argument the same as being right?
Socrates says nobody does wrong on purpose; they just make mistakes about what is good. Do you agree?
Is it worse to be unkind, or to have someone be unkind to you? Why might Socrates say the first?
Protagoras says Zeus gave justice to everyone. Why might it matter that everyone, not just experts, has a sense of fairness?
Which would you rather be good at: speaking well or knowing a lot? Could you have both?
